analysis.one_liner: Blocks new Arctic oil leases off Alaska until science and spill-response standards are met.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; it got no hearing and no vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped the Interior Department from selling or preparing to sell oil and gas leases in two Arctic waters off Alaska — the Chukchi and Beaufort Sea planning areas — until four conditions were met. Interior would first have to commission an independent National Research Council review of what science is missing, resolve the question of whether the polar bear should be protected under the Endangered Species Act, show that equipment exists that can recover at least 85 percent of any oil spilled in those waters, and determine that drilling could go forward without substantial harm to wildlife or Alaska Native subsistence hunting and fishing. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which took no action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would have protected Arctic marine waters, wildlife such as the polar bear, and the Alaska Native communities that depend on subsistence hunting and fishing, by keeping new drilling off the table until independent science confirmed it could be done safely. It also would have given Congress the information it needs to oversee Arctic leasing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Arctic wildlife and Alaska Native subsistence communities

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Interior Department from offering leases, preleasing, seismic surveys, exploration plans, or development plans in the Chukchi or Beaufort Sea planning areas until four prerequisites are met [S3].

One prerequisite is a National Research Council agreement to identify missing information about the Arctic marine ecosystems, including effects of climate change, review the adequacy of existing environmental, public health, and cultural studies, and report its findings and recommendations to Congress [S2] [S3].

Another prerequisite requires the Secretary to determine that mechanical oil spill response technologies exist that are documented to recover at least 85 percent of oil spilled under Chukchi and Beaufort Sea conditions — a standard aimed at the difficulty of cleaning up oil in icy Arctic waters [S3].

The bill also requires resolution of the polar bear's Endangered Species Act status, either a listing with designated critical habitat or a published determination that listing is not warranted, before leasing can proceed [S2] [S3].

Finally, the Secretary must determine that exploration and development can proceed without substantial adverse impact to wildlife, wildlife habitat, or subsistence, and that mitigation measures are identified and proven effective [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the bill would have deferred revenue and drilling opportunities in the Arctic to oil and gas companies, delaying any development in the Chukchi and Beaufort seas until the scientific and safety conditions were satisfied. Taxpayers would fund the National Research Council study. Consumers could face costs if Arctic development were delayed in a tight energy market, though Arctic offshore oil is a small share of national supply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking Arctic leases

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a high bar before any lease can even be offered: a spill-response technology documented to recover at least 85 percent of spilled oil, a standard that may be very difficult or impossible to meet in Arctic conditions, which in practice could block leasing indefinitely rather than just delay it [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: restricting new Arctic leasing defers domestic oil and gas production at a time when energy prices and energy security were major public concerns in 2008 [S3].
The requirements add new studies, determinations, and reporting that would take time and federal money before any economic activity could begin [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — protecting fragile Arctic waters, wildlife, and subsistence communities from the risk of a hard-to-clean oil spill, and forcing a rigorous independent science review first — were large but conditional and long-term. The costs were deferral of potential domestic oil production and study expenses, modest relative to national supply. The design leans toward caution: it does not ban drilling outright, but the 85 percent oil-recovery requirement is demanding enough that it could function as a practical moratorium. That trade-off is exactly what the Senate never debated, because the bill died in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kerry introduced the bill on January 29, 2008, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S1] [S5].
Four senators signed on as cosponsors: three Democrats and one Independent [S4].
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the bill expired [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies that wanted to lease and drill in the Chukchi and Beaufort seas were better off: with the bill dead, no new conditions stood between them and the leasing process. The Bush administration was free to proceed with Arctic lease sales without the independent science review, the polar-bear condition, or the spill-recovery standard the bill would have required.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies seeking Arctic drilling leases

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies (Arctic offshore exploration)
industries.note: The bill would have blocked lease sales, preleasing, seismic work, and exploration or development plans in the Chukchi and Beaufort seas until science and spill-response conditions were met, deferring the companies' access to Arctic reserves. A spill in these icy, remote waters would be very hard to clean up, so the industry's gain from fast leasing runs against the public's interest in protection. With the bill dead, leasing could proceed on the administration's timeline instead.

The bill conditions any leasing on a determination that drilling would not substantially harm subsistence, and requires the science review to account for subsistence activities. These communities had the most direct stake in keeping oil development out of the waters they hunt and fish.
